item.title: I switched from Phone Link to KDE Connect, and Windows 11 is missing these 4 game-changing features
item.itunes:title: I switched from Phone Link to KDE Connect, and Windows 11 is missing these 4 game-changing features
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
One of the many flagship features Microsoft touts for Windows 11 is the cross-device connectivity you get between your PC and your phone, specifically if it's running Android. And it's true that there are some cool things you can do with a setup like this, but it's also still very limited.

Meanwhile, KDE Connect has been around for a good while now, and it still offers capabilities Windows 11 can't or won't. Here are just a few of the features that should make you consider setting up KDE Connect.

Control my PC's media playback

Yes, it goes both ways

Windows 11's Phone Link lets you see plenty of info from your phone on your PC, and, to be fair to Microsoft, that does include media playback. That means I can play and pause a song from my PC, or skip a track if I want to. However, this only goes one way, meaning I can only control my phone from my PC.

KDE Connect extends this to go both ways, meaning I can also control something being played on my PC using my phone. I'd argue this is even more useful than the other way around, since I can use it while my PC is connected to a big screen, or if I'm moving around and the house with music playing from my computer.

Interestingly, the PC's music playback even integrates into Android's built-in system-wide music controls, so I can play/pause from my notification panel.

This two-way communication applies to most things, so it's not just music playback, but things like notifications. I can see my phone's on my PC, but I can also see my PC's on my phone.

Use a makeshift touchpad

Who needs a mouse?

I'll admit it's probably not the most common scenario, but if you've ever had to use a PC without a mouse or touchpad, or you simply want to get some distance from the PC and still be able to control it, KDE Connect has you covered too. When you link up a phone and a PC, you can use your phone as a touchpad to control the mouse on your computer, and you can even type using your phone's keyboard app.

Again, if you have a laptop connected to a TV, for example, this could let you control the computer without having to get up from the couch. Plus, the two-way communication also matters here, as you can also use your PC's mouse to interact with your phone, and type using the physical keyboard, so you can send messages this way. It's admittedly not the most convenient setup, but it does work, and it's another thing Windows wouldn't let you do by itself.

I turned my old Android phone into a Windows 11 touchpad, and my desk setup finally makes sense

Repurpose an Android for productivity.

1
By  Brian Burgess

On that note, you can also send clipboard content from your phone to your PC and vice versa. Your Windows clipboard is automatically synced to your phone, but to share it the other way around you need to manually push that content due to how Android permissions work.

Manage slideshow presentations

A presentation remote with an unexpected twist

If you've ever had to do a presentation in public, you know how much easier and more professional they can look when you have a proper presentation remote, rather than scurrying back to your computer to move on to the next slide. Microsoft used to provide a remote tool with its own Office suite, but that's no longer available.

KDE Connect brings that back and makes it even better, at least in terms of compatibility. This is because, unlike Microsoft's old solution, KDE Connect works with other Office software such as OnlyOffice, and in fact, you can use it with any software, to an extent.

NotebookLM helped me fix my PowerPoint presentations, and taught me how to do them better

I used NotebookLM to draft my presentations, and it ended up coaching me into a better storyteller

By  Beatrice Manuel

One of the best features of the remote in KDE Connect is that you can also use a virtual pointer to highlight content on the screen, and in a strange twist, it actually uses your phone's motion sensor. You simply hold down the pointer button on your phone, and move it as you would with a real pointer to highlight whatever you want. And since it's independent from any presentation software, you can do this even if you're presenting something else. Of course, moving a presentation back and forth still requires an Office app.

Run terminal commands

Quickly launch apps or perform maintenance tasks

Another big thing KDE Connect can do is run terminal commands on my PC with a single tap. I can add any command I want to the list on my PC, and simply tap it on my phone to run it.

How useful this is will naturally depend on your use case and your creativity, but I was able to use it to run a winget upgrade command to update all the apps on my PC, or simply launch an app. You could add commands for maintenance tasks, or even something as simple as shutting down or rebooting your PC.

These Windows terminal commands fix what Settings can't, and I use them every time my PC breaks

From update errors to internet issues, these commands save me every time.

By  Kazim Alvi

This is likely the most versatile aspect of this connection, though that also means it's the one where everyone will see a different use case. For some people, it may not be worth much at all, but for others, it could be a game changer. Still, the fact remains Windows 11 wouldn't let you do something like this out of the box.

KDE Connect is seriously impressive

I mostly focused on the unique features of KDE Connect here, but of course, it can also handle some things you'd expect, like basic notification syncing, making calls, or sending SMS messages from your PC. It's a very robust tool, and it's made even better when you realize it can also run on Linux.

item.title: I added live weather radar to Android Auto, and it changed how I plan my drives
item.itunes:title: I added live weather radar to Android Auto, and it changed how I plan my drives
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Most of us check the weather perhaps once in the morning when we're planning out our daily outfit. That works fine enough until a downpour completely derails your journey. Where I live, when it rains, it pours.

Moreover, since most of my driving is measured in hundreds of miles on the expressway, knowing the kind of weather I'm driving into can mean the difference between pulling over to the side of the expressway and riding out the storm at a rest stop. I'll always pick the latter. The problem is that while a weather forecast can tell me rain is expected, it can't tell me whether that rain is heading my way and when I am expected to barrel into it.

That's why I pulled up a weather app on my car's Android Auto headunit that tells me precisely that. The app puts this weather information on the car display and lets me cycle through everything from a live wind-view dashboard to a rain radar, so I can check what's happening around me without reaching for my phone. It's one of the coolest things I've added to my Android Auto setup in a while.

4 lesser-known Android Auto apps that are surprisingly useful

The more you know.

By  Chandraveer Mathur

I use the weather radar to decide when to leave

A weather radar gives me insights into what's happening around me

Having live weather data on your car's infotainment system changes how you approach any drive. The biggest change is that I no longer treat the weather forecast as a simple go, no-go answer. If the forecast suggests that it might rain later in the evening, that doesn't mean I should expect rain throughout the evening. The app's weather radar, on the other hand, gives me a better idea of what is happening right now. In fact, it can even show me a real-time visualization of cloud movements.

This is surprisingly useful when I have somewhere to be and when the weather doesn't look particularly favorable. Even before I start a drive, I just tap open the Weather & Radar app on Android Auto. Sometimes I even leave it open while I'm driving. This screen combines precipitation with other weather information and shows how ambient conditions are developing.

Beyond that, it works like a weather app, and what you get out of it depends on how you use it. For example, if I see dark clouds right outside and moving toward me, I know I have a decision to make.

I can either head toward my destination or pull over. If the clouds aren't represented as particularly dark and grey, it might just be a light shower. That's much more useful information than simply seeing an indication that it might rain.

I can see what's coming along on my drive

The extra radar layers are useful, even if they're not particularly necessary

While having a weather radar on your car's infotainment system can be useful for city driving, the real benefit is, predictably, on longer journeys. Most weather apps can only show conditions at specific locations, not along a route. That's just not a thing unless you start looking at cloud visualizations.

Having a weather radar in Android Auto means that it effectively follows your route. You can zoom in and scroll anytime during a stop. This lets you see the weather system ahead of you and observe if it is moving towards my route or away from it. These visualizations are updated by the minute, so you can be sure you are getting up-to-date information to make a more informed decision.

If you want to get granular, the app offers a number of different visualizations. The temperature radar is one of these. Let's say I'm driving into the hills; I can see the temperature difference between the plains and the hills. Honestly, let's be real, there's no practical benefit to this. But it certainly is cool.

Finally, it helps that the app loads up quickly. You probably wouldn't want a weather radar on your screen all the time. A navigation app is better suited to it. Most of the time, I have Google Maps or an offline navigation app like Organic Maps running on screen. But I'll swap over to the weather radar anytime I'm stopping for a break, or every hour or two, in case I suspect a change in weather conditions. It works great.

Adding a weather radar to my Android Auto setup helps me see when the weather will actually impact my drive

Honestly, I didn't expect adding a weather radar to my Android Auto setup to be anything more than a gimmick. Turns out, I check it more often than I thought I would. It solves a very specific problem for me and will for anyone who lives in an area where weather conditions change frequently. The app bridges the gap between knowing the forecast and knowing when it will impact me.

Weather & Radar

The Weather & Radar app allows you to display a weather, temperature and wind radar on your Android Auto display.

See at Google Play Store

item.title: Old enterprise servers are the worst way to start a Proxmox homelab, and a retired office PC beats them on almost everything
item.itunes:title: Old enterprise servers are the worst way to start a Proxmox homelab, and a retired office PC beats them on almost everything
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Proxmox is quite the solution for running virtualized services, including those part of a home lab. The allure of creating a home-based data center can be difficult to resist, especially when used enterprise hardware can be bought at a severe discount. ECC RAM, Multiple Ethernet ports. Remote management. These are the sort of features that aren't typically found elsewhere, but something like a Dell PowerEdge R21o II can tick all the right boxes.

I'm here to tell you that you should skip this step altogether and pick up a retired business desktop PC.

Enterprise gear is almost too appealing

Don't let yourself fall into the same trap I did

ECC RAM is just one of the advantages something like the PowerEdge R210 II offers. It has capable Xeon server support, Intel NICs for reliable connectivity, iDRAC for remote management, and is inside a rackmount chassis that's designed for continuous operation. It feels like a server, which is something a mini PC or used desktop simply cannot replicate. Installing Proxmox on the PowerEdge server felt like I was creating a miniature datacenter.

This is why used enterprise hardware (servers, switches, etc.) is such a common homelab topic. item.title: Fast Startup is the first setting I turn off on every Windows PC, and it's fixed more weird bugs than I expected
item.itunes:title: Fast Startup is the first setting I turn off on every Windows PC, and it's fixed more weird bugs than I expected
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Windows has improved a lot over the years, both in performance and stability. You don't get as many errors as you used to, and better memory management makes the whole experience feel more streamlined. But it's not the perfect operating system. There are things you still need to change on a new Windows install, from removing bloatware to reconfiguring default settings. And one such default setting I disable on every Windows PC is Fast Startup.

Fast Startup has been a part of the operating system since Windows 8, and while it helped at the time, the feature no longer feels relevant and can sometimes even be counterproductive. It's often the underlying cause behind weird bugs and errors. If you look through Windows troubleshooting guides online, you'll often find that disabling Fast Startup is among the suggested solutions. And there's a good reason for it.

I’m a power user and I’m disabling these Windows features on purpose

If you've used Windows 11 for any length of time, you'll understand.

8
By  Korbin Brown

Fast Startup improves boot time

But at the expense of system stability

Fast Startup, as the name suggests, is a Windows feature designed to speed up your computer's boot time. It works much like the hibernation feature, but instead of saving the entire session to the drive, Fast Startup only saves the kernel session and loaded drivers to the hiberfil.sys file. This way, when you turn on the computer, it boots faster because it doesn't have to load the kernel session and drivers from scratch. Since it can save you a few seconds every time you turn on the PC, Windows enables the feature by default. But there's a problem!

With Fast Startup enabled, your PC doesn't truly shut down, and it hasn't done so in years. It just reloads the previous state, and if that's buggy, the issue carries over to the next session. That's why you often see people suggesting restarting the PC as a troubleshooting step rather than shutting it down and turning it back on. Because Fast Startup doesn't apply to restarts.

That's not it; there are other problems, too. For example, sometimes driver or Windows updates that require a true restart fail to install when Fast Startup is enabled. Even Microsoft, in a support article for Windows 10, notes that Fast Startup could be why users have trouble installing updates. Apart from that, on dual-boot systems, say when running Linux alongside Windows, Fast Startup can cause a wide array of problems, from network issues to data corruption. You may also notice your laptop automatically waking up from sleep.

More importantly, your PC needs a full shutdown every once in a while. This power cycles the components, which is essential, and Windows boots in a fresh state without carrying over any bugs from the previous session. That's why you should disable Fast Startup, especially if you're experiencing these bugs.

5 ways to make Windows 11 boot faster without new hardware

If you have a Windows 11 PC that feels like it boots slower than it should, try some of these tips.

5
By  Adam Conway

Disabling Fast Startup is easy

And you are generally better off without it

You can easily disable Fast Startup in Windows 11 and Windows 10. The steps are the same on both iterations, since the feature is still accessible through the Control Panel and hasn't been moved to the Settings app.

To turn off Fast Startup, launch the Control Panel, go into System and Security, click Change what the power buttons do under Power Options, then Change settings that are currently unavailable, uncheck Turn on fast startup, and finally click on Save changes. That's it. And if you ever decide to re-enable the feature, the steps are the same, but you will need to check the Fast Startup option instead.

I cut my Windows boot time in half by running one simple command, and you can too

It was free and saved me from buying a new SSD.

20
By  Jasmine Mannan

Some may still benefit from Fast Startup

Though it's not as relevant anymore

So far, we have discussed the downsides of Fast Startup, but the feature still serves (or served) a purpose. Otherwise, Microsoft wouldn't have added Fast Startup and enabled it by default. Keep in mind that Fast Startup was introduced when PCs still primarily had HDDs. Since those drives weren't as fast, the feature helped reduce boot time.

But as SSDs became mainstream, Fast Startup lost its relevance. SSDs are already fast enough, and the feature doesn't make that big a difference to boot time anymore. You can still save a few seconds during boot, but the weird bugs and issues it introduces simply make it a bad deal for most users.

However, if you aren't facing any problems and your computer still has an HDD, you can leave Fast Startup turned on. In that case, you can periodically use the shutdown /s /f /t 0 command to completely shut down the system. That gives your computer a fresh start any time you want.

I ditched most of the Windows start-up chaos and sped up my boot times without any third-party tools, here's how

Cleaning up startup tasks can make a world of difference

By  João Carrasqueira

I should have disabled it sooner

Fast Startup is a clear example of how Windows defaults aren't always the best choice, at least not for the vast majority of users. It may work for a smaller set, but most people are better off without it. I've found Fast Startup to be the cause of issues on my Windows laptops on countless occasions. Earlier, I used to temporarily disable the feature and then re-enable it once the problem disappeared. But now that both my laptops feature SSDs and are fast enough, I see no point in leaving it turned on. And believe me, I have faced far fewer issues since then.

item.title: Intel had the 16GB GPU the market desperately needed, but decided not to ship it
item.itunes:title: Intel had the 16GB GPU the market desperately needed, but decided not to ship it
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Shopping for a 16GB GPU in 2026 has become a really grim affair. The RTX 5060 Ti 16GB "launched" at a price of $429, and now sells for around $800, and the RX 9060 XT is a bit better, but paying over $500 for a card that launched at $349 is also suboptimal. Right now, if you're looking for a brand-new card that has 16GB of VRAM and you're on a budget, those are basically your only two choices.

Intel does have the 12GB Arc B580 that has been a budget champion of its generation, but it's not competing with the likes of the 5060 Ti and 9060 XT. However, they did have a B770 in the works, but unfortunately for us, it never reached store shelves in a configuration that makes sense for the average consumer. It was the card the market needed, but never got.

Intel's Arc B580 is great for budget gamers, except for one major flaw

Budget GPUs seemingly have a champion in the Arc B580, if only it didn't tank with budget CPUs.

11
By  Tanveer Singh

16GB choices at this tier of GPU have collapsed into two choices

The 5060 Ti and the 9060 XT stand alone

When it comes to the mid-range performance class, there are really only two choices, and both of them are inflated in price. Nvidia's option is the RTX 5060 Ti 16GB, which has nearly doubled from its $429 launch price to about $800 at major US retailers. AMD's is the RX 9060 XT 16GB, a $349 card at launch whose cheapest models now sit at around $520, with plenty of partner cards well beyond that.

The Radeon is a much better value pick, but that's part of the problem. The 9060 XT 16GB doesn't have a competitor near its price, and it still seems to be rising. Intel, meanwhile, isn't apart of this range at all. Its gaming lineup tops out at the Arc B580, a 12GB card that launched at $249. There's nothing above it for anyone who wants more memory or more performance from Intel.

I'd rather buy an older high-end GPU than a newer low-end one, and VRAM is only part of why

Built to last

3
By  Ty Sherback

Intel has had the chip made, and we know how it performs

The B770 "exists" but it's not on a consumer card

The B770 was expected to use Intel's larger Battlemage chip, BMG-G31, with 32 Xe cores against the B580's 20, and 16GB of GDDR6. That chip did end up launching in a graphics card as the Arc Pro B70. That card had 32GB of memory and was built around AI and workstation use, not gaming.

People have picked one up and used it for gaming purposes though, so we know roughly what a B770 would've been able to achieve in today's games. TechSpot's dozen-game suite had it roughly matching the RX 9060 XT and about 6% behind the RTX 5060 Ti. That puts it a bit short of the early rooms that put it between the RTX 4070 and 5070. There are even gaming support for the drivers powering the Pro B70 and B65, so the foundation exists for these chips to be capable gaming cards.

Intel's B580 GPU shows how much AMD has dropped the ball with Radeon

How are you going to let a newcomer show you up on their second kick at the can?

7
By  Ty Sherback

Intel's reasons for skipping it are valid

It's clear that they wouldn't have been able to compete on the other metrics

For a die that's RTX 5080-sized, only being able to deliver 5060 Ti-class performance is a tough look for what would've been the B770, and that's just the start of its issues. Being that size means it's significantly more expensive to make, and at the board power numbers coming out of the Arc Pro B70, it's clear that it would've be fighting to keep up efficiency-wise too.

Pricing is the real key, because nobody is going to pay a premium for an Intel GPU. The absolute maximum a B770 could've been is $400 to undercut the 5060 Ti's $429 MSRP, and to sell a chip of its size at that price, it's almost certainly not worth it. Using GDDR6 wouldn't have saved it either, as evidenced by the price increases that the RX 9000 series has experienced due to memory shortages.

The Arc Pro B70 is currently well over $1,000 at the time of writing, and the extra 16GB of GDDR7X on-board simply cannot account for the entirety of the $700 gulf between it and the alleged B770.

Intel Arc B580 vs RTX 5060 Ti: the real mid-range GPU you should buy

In the battle of mid-range GPUs, should you stick with Nvidia or opt for Intel's Arc B580?

3
By  Madeline Ricchiuto

Shipping it anyway could've been valuable

More options are always good

What's good for Intel's margins and what's good for people buying graphics cards are different questions, though, and the B770, even if it were overpriced at MSRP, could've been competitive at elevated prices. It's anyone's guess as to what it would've sold for, but if it were to slide in at the gap between the RX 9060 and RTX 5060 Ti, it would've given buyers a nice middle ground. Of course, this would be dependent on its performance.

The Intel Arc B770 is dead, long live the Arc B770

Intel's mid-range Battlemage GPU has been shelved, but it's not completely gone

15
By  Tanveer Singh

The gap isn't being filled anytime soon

Leaks suggest that Intel's Xe3P "Celestial" gaming card was canceled long ago, making the B580 and B570 Intel's only discrete gaming GPUs for the foreseeable future. No new gaming cards are expected from Intel until at least late 2027 with its "Druid" GPUs, the fate of which is still undecided.

item.title: The best thing about Debian is how old all of its software is
item.itunes:title: The best thing about Debian is how old all of its software is
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Debian’s old software is often discussed as its biggest weakness when compared to other distros. But when I picked Debian for my own home server, I specifically chose it because of those years-old versions. I am running bare-metal Debian on an old business laptop with more than 20 stacks, and Debian is the least concerning element in the homelab, and that sounds the opposite for software this old.

What "old" actually means in Debian Stable

The version number says one thing. The patch log says another.

I am running Debian 12.15 Bookworm on an 8-year-old business laptop, which I repurposed as my home server. As of Oct 7, 2026, the latest 6.1 kernel upstream is 6.1.189, but mine is at 6.1.187-1. And the upstream stable is at 7.2.9 against my 6.1. It is neither an accident nor negligence; this is how Debian Stable works in practice.

If you are on Debian, you already know about the Debian freeze model. The concept is simple: when Debian releases, it locks the package version at that time, and for future fixes it usually doesn't bump the version; instead, it backports the fixes into that version. So, the version now labels the base, not the patched number.

I first saw it working with OpenSSH and a few more packages. If you own a server, one of the first things you install is OpenSSH. It's a good test case because it is the front door to a server. Even though my server wasn’t headless, I still installed it because most of the time, the laptop is kept in a corner, away from my workstation.

Debian Bookworm was released in early 2023, and OpenSSH was at 9.2p1 when it came out. I installed Debian last year in 2025, and the package is still on 9.2p1 for me, even though the upstream is now at 10.6. But this doesn’t mean it's unpatched; the same base was revised with tens of updates on top, in my case from deb12u1 to deb12u10.

Those backports fixed various security concerns like the regreSSHion (CVE-2024-6387), Terrapin (CVE-2023-48795), plus three other CVEs. It isn't only OpenSSH; the same behavior can be tracked with other packages on the host too. Like Git (Debian: 2.39.5, upstream: 2.56.0).

But the model has a boundary, and it depends on Debian. Some software is either too old or changes too much to backport and is difficult to maintain within the old stable base. I found a few packages on the host myself after running Debian's own tool ‘check-support-status’; it flagged several packages, like webkit2gtk, that aren’t being maintained and backported to Bookworm.

While writing this article, I checked my pending updates, and there were hundreds. But it doesn’t mean Debian isn’t doing its part; it was me who was behind the updates. A simple full-upgrade command did the magic.

Debian's next release just made it near-impossible for tampered binaries to sneak onto your PC

Reproducible packages are here to stay.

1
By  Simon Batt

What Stable actually bought my homelab

Every layer above Debian has broken on me. Debian hasn't.

I run more than 20 stacks on the Debian machine. Most of them are deployed via Portainer; a few are deployed directly on the host, but that is not the point here. I always say self-hosting comes in two parts: deploying the container and maintaining it.

Over the last year of homelabbing, most of them have broken at some point, and I fixed them, but those were always above the operating-system layer, not Debian. I am not claiming that Debian is unbreakable, but for me, nearly every time, the troubleshooting was done on the container layer.

There were around 228 pending updates when I checked today; the oldest dates back a few months, but did they give me any issues? No. The last few issues I can remember are Watchtower auto-update breakage, Portainer update orphaning a volume, NetBird rewriting the resolv.conf file, and AdGuard Home detaching itself from its bridge.

And all those issues were diagnosed and fixed without technically touching Debian itself. For example, Watchtower, while its routine task updated my Immich and Nextcloud containers, was in no way related to Debian. The same is true for other incidents.

The point here is that the software running above the operating system keeps moving, and each still survives every change because the foundation underneath it remains unchanged. The NetBird incident may be connected to the host because, when it modified the files, the apt and git operations temporarily broke, but NetBird is a third-party package from its own repository and is responsible for the resolver change, not Debian.

All the 20+ stacks sitting on top of Debian came back online even after a 228-package upgrade, a new kernel, and a reboot, and that is the whole point.

My outdated Windows 10 PC was headed for the recycling bin until Proxmox gave it a second life

This dinosaur machine now runs my LLMs inside an LXC

4
By  Ayush Pande

Where old software starts to hurt

The old software was fine. My habits weren't.

Honestly, I didn’t pay a major cost for the software being old itself. My machine didn’t break because of some ancient package. One minor cost was on me: I allowed 228 upgrades to pile up. Two reasons: first, I didn’t look for those upgrades. Second, I never installed unattended-upgrades. The system kept running normally and didn’t ask for any attention; that’s why I stopped checking on it.

Unsupported packages put the system at risk. If Debian can no longer maintain the software, the responsibility falls on me to remove, replace, or accept the risk. For instance, the same tool also flagged a few packages as end-of-support, like libmfx1 (2024-11-21) and libmbedcrypto7 (2026-06-12).

This doesn’t mean that, since Debian ended support for them, the libraries have become inherently vulnerable. The tool only flagged those two ended ones. The rest, like checking the actual changelogs and deciding what to do, are on me. The freeze model is an excellent pro for Debian, but it doesn’t make an indefinite maintenance promise.

For me specifically, the server isn’t a minimal headless installation. Since it is a laptop with a working screen, I installed the full XFCE desktop above it. And the packages installed manually, such as task-desktop, task-xfce-desktop, task-laptop, and task-ssh-server, are my choice, not Debian's.

The best habit is to move the external packages as fast as possible. And let Debian Stable do what it is best at.

Linux was almost called Freax, and someone renamed it without asking Linus

It was a close call.

1
By  Simon Batt

The boring part is a choice

Even though Debian 13 Trixie is already available, I don’t have any immediate plans to upgrade, because I know bookworm is already on Long Term Support (LTS) until mid-2028. Debian’s software age is acceptable because it lets me decide which part of my homelab I want to keep moving and which part can stay put. The slow-moving changes make my life easier, and I can actually focus on the container layer of the homelab. I want the 20+ stacks to be the interesting part, not the operating system underneath.

item.title: Windows Task Manager still speaks a language that's probably older than you are, but there's a reason why
item.itunes:title: Windows Task Manager still speaks a language that's probably older than you are, but there's a reason why
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
You would have used Task Manager on your Windows PC countless times, whether to terminate a stuck application or reduce your startup app clutter. Windows 11's Task Manager has evolved considerably over the last three decades, but it can be traced back to the first version shipped with Windows NT 4.0 in 1996. It succeeded a more basic utility called "Task List" seen on earlier Windows versions.

What's interesting is that the modern Task Manager still reports on the ideas tied to Windows NT's virtual memory system. Some of the terminology it uses was designed in an era when memory capacity was scarce, measured in megabytes instead of gigabytes. It was a time when aggressively managing the physical memory and deciding what was offloaded to disk wasn't optimization; it was required to keep the system stable.

I replaced Windows Task Manager with this free tool—and I'm never going back

This lightweight alternative gives me more control, information and security

1
By  Abhinav Raj

"Committed" memory is a holdover from an assumption that's not true anymore

We have a different type of RAM scarcity in this day and age

If you open the "Performance" tab in Task Manager and click on "Memory," you'll see a header called "Committed" next to other numbers below the graphs on the right pane. This refers to "commit charge," or the total amount of virtual memory the OS has promised the system applications in the form of physical memory and the page file on the disk. It includes the amount of virtual memory already in use by running applications.

This nomenclature and the architecture underneath made a lot of sense when RAM was the scarcest resource on the system (not the way it is in 2026) and swapping programs to the hard drive wasn't optional. Doing so was the only way to keep multiple programs running at once, irrespective of the performance penalty of swapping to disk. Although your modern Windows PC still works technically the same way, the underlying premise has shifted considerably.

Modern systems with 32GB of RAM are rarely struggling for physical memory, even with multiple applications running at once. And the penalty associated with swapping to a fast NVMe SSD is nowhere close to what it was in the time of conventional hard drives. So, the terminology was never updated even though the scarcity it was built around largely disappeared.

4 lesser-known Windows features that help make your PC faster

Sometimes, simple changes make the biggest difference

9
By  Kazim Alvi

"Paged pool" and "Non-paged pool" don't matter anymore

The average user doesn't need to think about it

The same "Memory" section will show you terms like "Paged pool" and "Non-paged pool." They refer to the system memory area that is allowed to be paged to the disk and the one that must always remain on physical RAM, respectively. This distinction is still in use today, but it is also a direct artifact of the same scarcity-era thinking.

It exists because deciding the programs that could never be paged out to disk was a meaningful engineering problem. Offloading critical programs to storage could be fatal or even impossible. Today, however, paged and non-paged pools are no more than internal bookkeeping for anyone trying to understand their system in Task Manager's "Performance" tab. It's still accurate, but not useful anymore.

Your PC gets slower the longer it stays on, and it’s not just your imagination

Your PC needs a proper power cycle once in a while

32
By  Tanveer Singh

"Handles" feels like terminology Windows never updated

No one has a handle on what it means

In the "CPU" section of the "Performance" tab, you can see a header called "Handles" next to "Speed," "Processes," and "Threads." It refers to the number of open references a process holds to system resources — files, registry keys, and more. Now, it can be a useful diagnostic in a specific scenario, such as a process with a high handle count indicating resource leaks.

However, the term and the object-handle system it reports on are typical Windows NT elements. "Handles" is essentially a low-level OS concept exposed to a mainstream, everyday monitoring tool without being translated to anything a casual user will understand. It could help an experienced user detect an anomaly, but it's a mid-90s OS concept that has stayed unchanged for three decades.

Microsoft has changed its product names so many times that there's a website to track them all

Has your favorite app changed its identity recently?

By  Simon Batt

Changing these terms isn't worth the disruption

Who would it benefit?

You may wonder why Microsoft hasn't bothered to update or at least rename these Task Manager terms to reflect the modern Windows architecture. It could help more users understand their systems better. The reason is that changing any of this risks breaking the communication chain with an established audience — IT admins, developers, and power users.

They have relied on these exact terms for decades for documentation, troubleshooting guides, forum threads, and knowledge banks. This terminology has stayed consistent going back to the days of Windows NT in the 90s. Renaming it would cause needless chaos across these domains without benefiting any casual users who ignore the deeper terms in the "Performance" tab anyway.

5 reasons Task Manager DeLuxe is a must-have for power users

It might not have all of the features, but it's easy to use and looks good.

11
By  Adam Conway

Task Manager can be helpful without a complete terminology update

Task Manager on Windows remains a useful monitoring and diagnostic tool despite some of its terms not making sense to a modern audience. Microsoft hasn't changed its legacy terminology because it's technically still true and maintains consistency with decades of documentation and power user familiarity.

item.title: Voicebox cloned my voice from a few seconds of audio on my own PC, and it's the most terrifying thing I've seen local AI do
item.itunes:title: Voicebox cloned my voice from a few seconds of audio on my own PC, and it's the most terrifying thing I've seen local AI do
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
A few months ago, when Kyutai released Pocket TTS, I was able to clone my own voice from a 5-second-long clip, which was an experience that left me wondering just how fragile the voice-based identity checks at banks and insurers had become. The barrier to access was so low that anyone with a PC and an internet connection could've followed the same steps and reached the same outcome.

A few months later, it seems that this very same process has gained a dedicated desktop application for Windows, Linux, and macOS, in the form of an open-source utility known as Voicebox. The installation is point-and-click, the results are much more convincing, and the entire thing can run on consumer hardware. Here's why it's equal parts impressive and equal parts frightening.

What is Voicebox?

What does it do, and who is it for?

  • Credit: Voicebox.sh
  • Credit: Voicebox.sh
  • Credit: Voicebox.sh
  • Credit: Voicebox.sh
  • Credit: Voicebox.sh
  • Credit: Voicebox.sh
  • Credit: Voicebox.sh
  • Credit: Voicebox.sh
  • Credit: Voicebox.sh
  • Credit: Voicebox.sh

Voicebox is an open-source and free-to-use voice studio created by Jamie Pine, who is the founder of Spacedrive Technology Inc. It is distributed under the MIT license, pitched as a local replacement for two paid services, including ElevenLabs for voice cloning and text-to-speech, and WisprFlow for dictation. Since it's open-source and everything runs on the hardware you own, using it doesn't require an account.

At the center of the app, of course, are its voice cloning capabilities, which is why I was interested in the app to begin with. A user can build a voice profile from an uploaded audio file, a microphone recording, or audio captured directly from whatever is playing on the user's PC, including a YouTube video or a Spotify podcast. From there, five of its speech engines, including Alibaba's Qwen3-TTS and Resemble AI's Chatterbox can read any typed text back in that voice across as many as 23 languages.

The core voice-cloning feature is surrounded by a comprehensive set of tools. Voicebox comes with a timeline editor for multi-voice projects, an effects rack, system-wide dictation powered by Whisper, and even a local API that lets coding agents speak back to you in a cloned voice.

Despite what it might seem like, there are plenty of legitimate reasons for using it. The utility is designed for everything from audiobook and podcast production to NPC dialogue, voice assistants, and various accessibility features.

That being said, as is obvious, there's enough potential for more malicious use-cases as well. Spacedrive's terms acknowledge that its voice-ownership checks are limited, and don't extend to the desktop application itself. This clearly means that there's nothing stopping someone from cloning another person's voice and using it for whatever purpose they may see fit without the safeguards that normally exist on a hosted service.

Llama.cpp, Speaches, and Open WebUI turned my Raspberry Pi into a voice assistant that actually works

The best part? This voice assistant runs entirely locally

By  Ayush Pande

How does Voicebox work?

And what you need to run it

Under the hood, Voicebox is essentially a desktop wrapper around a collection of local speech models. If you give it a voice sample, it's transcribed by Whisper, and then a speech engine such as Qwen3-TTS uses the audio and transcript to generate new speech in that voice. It all sounds complicated, but the app's UI makes using it a piece of cake. The only skill set you'd need to run this app is being able to boot a PC and run a setup wizard.

Voicebox's website says that as little as 3 seconds of audio is enough for voice cloning, but its docs recommend 10 to 30 seconds of clean speech for the best results. Either way, that's an absurdly low bar for anyone with a public-facing voice, given how much usable audio can be found through a YouTube interview, a podcast, or even an Instagram reel. It also makes responding to unknown callers riskier than usual, since all it takes for a cyber threat actor to record a few seconds of your voice to clone it.

There isn't much of a hardware barrier either. The requirements are 8GB of RAM, 5GB of storage, and a multicore CPU. The recommended requirements only go up to 16GB of system RAM and preferably an Nvidia GPU. Those are the specs that my Lenovo Legion 5 Pro laptop from 2022 already comes with, and that's where I tested the utility myself.

There were two other details buried in the patch notes that I thought were worth keeping in mind. Since version 0.4.5, cached models have been able to generate speech without an internet connection, while the most recent build, v0.5.0, dates back to April. Once everything is downloaded, nothing sits between you and the voice you're generating, which is something I tested myself.

I gave Qwen 3.8 27B a reverse-engineering job I assumed needed a frontier model, and it finished in 30 minutes

Qwen 3.8 27B genuinely shocked me with what it achieved here.

11
By  Adam Conway

Using Voicebox is fast, easy, and concerningly simple

It takes three steps, and you're done

The latest version of the Voicebox gives you three ways to get a voice cloned. You can upload an existing clip, record one through your microphone, or capture whatever is playing on your PC, although recordings and captures are capped at 30 seconds. You're then asked to provide the transcript for the recording, and from there, that's pretty much it. There's no identity check, ownership declaration, and nothing on the profile screen asking whether the voice actually belongs to you.

Before the first run, I needed a couple of downloads. The first was Qwen3-TTS 1.7B, which was about 3.6GB. The second was a separate CUDA backend for my laptop's RTX 3070 GPU, because Nvidia acceleration doesn't come bundled with the app. Once the two were installed, the whole process, right from recording my sample to generating the cloned voice took less than five minutes.

In regard to the results, it was downright fascinating to see how well the model was able to clone the characteristics of my voice. The cadence, pitch, and timbre were all carried over into a sentence that I had never spoken, with only a few imperfections giving away that it wasn't exactly me. Funnily enough, when I played the sample to three of my close friends, all three cited the same reason for being able to tell them apart, which was the absence of background noise in the generated clip.

It isn't perfect, but for cyber threat actors, it doesn't have to be

While almost certainly impressive (and I might add, unlike anything I've seen before), the output isn't completely indistinguishable from my voice. Acoustic anomalies associated with AI-generated voices are still present, and specialized deep learning detectors could certainly be able to distinguish the output from organic speech. The problem is that those tools aren't exactly sitting on the other end of a phone call for an unwitting recipient. To someone who doesn't interact with me regularly, the clone is convincing enough to pass as my voice.

item.title: My TV speakers were never the problem, and one audio setting fixed dialogue I couldn't hear
item.itunes:title: My TV speakers were never the problem, and one audio setting fixed dialogue I couldn't hear
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
I've been using a soundbar instead of my TV's onboard speakers for years because, well, the latter is rarely a good option. When I got this TV back in 2020, its speakers were serviceable for a while. After all, I finished The Last of Us Part 2 without ever buying a soundbar. That said, the TV speakers started showing their limits as soon as I watched a few movies and TV shows. The volume was fine, but the sound separation left a lot to be desired.

Overall, the audio experience was hollow, which prompted me to buy a soundbar a few months later. Recently, I was testing the soundbar on my PC, hoping to replace my existing PC audio setup and buy a new speaker system for the TV. This forced me to make do with the TV speakers for a few days, and I found out that they aren't as bad as I had thought, provided I tweaked a crucial setting.

I was content with seeing "Dolby Atmos" on the screen

The TV's speakers weren't equipped to handle it

For the first few hours without my soundbar, I assumed the TV speakers were doing the best they could. They weren't great to begin with, so the muddy audio I was hearing was expected. However, I glanced at the screen and saw that my Apple TV 4K was sending Dolby Atmos audio to the TV. This wasn't a surprise, considering I had picked that setting, but it worked well with the soundbar, not the TV speakers.

The muffled, inaudible dialogue was because the TV speakers couldn't process the incoming Atmos signal. Apple TV showed that Dolby Atmos was playing, but that only meant that it was sending that particular audio stream to the TV. Since the TV's speakers weren't equipped to handle the incoming multichannel bitstream, they downmixed it to stereo, creating a poor audio experience.

Checking my TV's audio settings made it clear — the audio output was set to "Pass Through." While this was ideal for a soundbar that could process Dolby Atmos, it was suboptimal for the TV's onboard speakers.

HDMI eARC is the only audio port on your TV that matters, yet most people plug their soundbar into the wrong one

Passing lossless audio to soundbars is a non-negotiable feature, and you need eARC for it

By  Tanveer Singh

Fixing the audio format mismatch is the key

Let the TV speakers receive a safe audio signal

It was time to change the video input to my Android TV and head into its audio settings. I had to pick an option that let the TV process the incoming audio from the Apple TV 4K properly. I changed the audio output from "Pass Through" to "PCM," which means Pulse Code Modulation. PCM is an uncompressed digital audio format that often converts the incoming audio to stereo format due to bandwidth limitations on older TVs.

Switching to PCM instantly made dialogue in movies and TV shows clearer. I was technically hearing an inferior audio signal now, stripped of object-based height effects, but my TV speakers weren't equipped for that anyway. At least, I could now make out dialogue properly and the soundstage was overall better.

If you have a modern TV with onboard speakers that support Dolby Atmos or other lossless audio formats, pick those output formats in the audio settings. Streaming apps typically send Dolby Digital instead of Dolby Atmos, but even that has surround-sound effects, which a capable TV can process natively.

You might have better luck with Dialogue Enhancement or Auto Volume

TV speakers need all the help they can get

Modern movie and TV audio is infamous for terrible audio mixing where people can't make out what the characters are saying half the time. This forces people to turn on subtitles or make do with their existing audio setup. Even after changing the audio format on your TV, you may still not hear the dialogue properly.

Thankfully, you have a few more settings to experiment with. The first is dialogue enhancement, which may have different names depending on your TV. On the Apple TV 4K, it's called Enhance Dialogue, but on your TV it might be called Clear Voice or Voice Enhancement. Turning this on isolates and boosts human speech frequencies, which should make dialogue clearer.

The other setting is called Auto Volume or Night Mode on different TV models. This setting compresses the audio signal to reduce the gap between loud and quiet moments, effectively preventing dialogue from getting buried under loud sounds. Note that these settings will suppress other sounds in the audio stream, so your overall experience may vary. Check how you like the results, and turn these settings off if you're not impressed.

I stopped chasing 4K and started fixing my audio, and films got better immediately

Better sound made my movies feel bigger than any 4K upgrade ever did

By  Samarveer Singh

My TV speakers are bad, but they can be improved

I had dismissed my TV's onboard speakers as terrible, but it turns out I could have made them decent with a few audio tweaks. The main change I made to improve the audio experience was changing the audio format. This lets the TV process the incoming audio in a format it could safely handle. Experiment with every audio setting on your TV to make the most of your TV speakers.

item.title: I connected Claude Code to Mermaid, and it replaced every diagramming app I ever used
item.itunes:title: I connected Claude Code to Mermaid, and it replaced every diagramming app I ever used
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Diagramming sounds like one of those tasks that should be quick, until you're trying to nudge the fourth box in place with arrows that refuse to line up, and 20 minutes have passed. Handing all that work to Claude is the obvious solution to the problem. This is exactly what I've been doing to get my diagram elements to line up perfectly in no time, and then I just save the files straight to my vault and open them in Obsidian Canvas or with the Excalidraw plugin.

Then I realized Claude had a Mermaid connector this whole time. Mermaid is both a diagramming tool and the text-based language the tool uses. Claude could already read and write this language, it just couldn't render interactive diagrams or pass them off to your Mermaid account before the connector.

What the Mermaid connector actually does in Claude

Think of it as a drawing inside the chat

Mermaid works by having you write out in text which box points to which, and its app turns that text into a picture, basically. Claude is fluent in the language, and even though I've become familiar with some of the Mermaid syntax over the years, it's not something I now have to fully memorize anymore.

The connector is what Anthropic calls an MCP App, meaning it can show a live interface in the conversation instead of just replying with text. With the Mermaid MCP, Claude writes the diagram text, the connector passes it along, and a widget in the chat draws it with the Mermaid library. The widget has a copy button for the text as well.

Behind the widget there are seven tools which Claude sorts into groups. Claude can call four of them itself. Display is the main one, since it's what draws the diagram in the chat, and sign-in connects your Mermaid account. The other two let Claude see what's in that account: one lists your saved diagrams and the other reads a diagram's code from a link. The remaining three are labeled app-only. One repairs a diagram with a syntax error, one saves a diagram to your account, and the last one updates a diagram that's already saved there.

Just noting that simply adding the official Mermaid connector only gave me one tool at first. So I added the newer server as a custom connector using Mermaid's v3 URL: https://chatgpt.mermaid.ai/anthropic/v3/mcp.

I borrowed Claude prompts from Anthropic engineers and immediately stopped wasting time on bad ones

The best prompts come from the team.

By  Mahnoor Faisal

Claude already speaks Mermaid, so why even bother with the connector?

Adding the Mermaid connector has perks

Claude already reads and writes Mermaid, so the obvious objection could be, why even bother with the connector at all? You can simply get Claude to generate the text and paste it into any Mermaid tool.

What the connector does mostly ties Claude into Mermaid's tools and account. So you can pass off diagrams straight to your Mermaid account, and if the syntax has an error, the widget offers to repair it. Keep in mind that generating, rendering, and reading Mermaid diagrams is free, but repairing will use your Mermaid AI credits.

The bigger difference for me, however, is that this connector gives you a direct way into Mermaid's own editor. The widget can open the diagram in your browser (which will require you to be signed in with your account), and you can keep iterating on it with Mermaid's editor. There's now also a visual editor, and the code updates as you edit visually (at least for flowcharts). And the file exports in a few formats, one of them being the raw Mermaid text.

Saving goes through the widget as well, and an update overwrites the diagram already in your account instead of making a copy. Claude can also pull a diagram in from its link, so something could go from the chat to Mermaid's editor and back again. Just be mindful of how much you generate because your plan still comes into the picture - the Basic plan stops at three diagrams, with limited AI use on top.

Mermaid is the best Obsidian feature you didn't know about

Visualize your thinking using mermaid diagrams in Obsidian

1
By  Parth Shah

Flowcharts are only the start
